Sorry but #4 is not exactly true. Heroin may have downstream effects to the "pleasure centers" of your brain but not in the same way sugar does, I mean......opiates do a hell of a lot more than just stimulate those few parts of the brain.

I hate when I see something like this because I can't ever be sure that all the "facts" are true.....without spending time finding that out since I am lazy.
But it is still effecting it the same way right? Just opiates hit you much harder.

No. There are specific receptors in your brain that opiates attach to that nothing else does besides what the body produces (endogenous opioids). Sugar may cause a surge of dopamine in certain parts of the brain but that is all it does in terms of addiction and it is short lived. Tolerance to sugar may build in some ways but never to the point of crippling withdrawal.

Opiates not only cause this surge of dopamine (on a much larger scale) but they also activate the endogenous opioid receptors in your brain that are responsible for perception of pain (physical and psychological, the brain doesn't really differentiate in this case), appetite, mood, libido, hormone production, gut motility, internal drive or motivation, pleasure derived from accomplishing a task or goal, etc etc etc. Activating these receptors cause downstream release of dopamine as well, but like I said above.....on a scale that can't really be compared to sugar.

Also, ain't nobody sucking dicks for gummy bears.

Alcohol is kinda cool because it works differently then a lot of common recreational drugs. First of all it starts being absorbed in the stomach (most drugs have to make it to the small intestine first), and once it reaches your blood stream alcohol will diffuse to pretty much every cell in your body. Unlike say.....weed.....which is limited in what it CAN effect and what it does effect. Alcohol pretty much affects everything.

As for what alcohol does specifically.....well that my friend is where you have to learn! In order to understand what alcohol does you need to read up on the structure of a neuron and understand how signalling works (undergraduate stuff, no need to learn all the receptor subtypes and all their potential effects). Once you know the difference between an excitatory and inhibitory synaptic potential it is pretty easy. That and learning what the different groups of neurotransmitters are and what they do.

I know that coursera does psychopharmacology classes for free online, I have heard they are pretty good. If that is not your cup of tea I would find out what text books most biopsychology/psychopharmacolgy classes use and just read those suckers front to back!

I know you can find textbooks on torrent sites now so really even just searching for "psychopharmacology" or "introduction to psychopharmacolgy" should give you a textbook that will teach you most of what you want to know! Besides going to school to become a doctor/researcher/pharmacist......this is the easier and much more fun way of going about this!
